opus-5.5.text:
I think the data wall is real, but I don't think it's the end of the road. It's more of a forcing function. For the last several years, the recipe has been fairly simple: take more high-quality human-generated text, train a bigger model, and you get predictably better results. At some point you exhaust the easily accessible, high-quality data on the internet, and the returns from just scraping more start to diminish. So yes, that particular axis of scaling is going to slow down.

But what that does, in my view, is shift the emphasis toward other ways of turning compute into intelligence. Coming from a background in reinforcement learning and working on systems like AlphaGo, AlphaZero, and MuZero, the lesson we learned again and again is that you don't necessarily need more human data if you have a way for the system to generate its own experience and get a signal about what's good. AlphaZero never saw a single human game, and it surpassed everything that had been trained on human data. The bottleneck there wasn't data, it was compute and having a good environment with a clear reward.

So I think the next phase is about synthetic data, self-play, and reinforcement learning on top of these pretrained models. You use the model to generate candidate solutions, reasoning traces, code, proofs, and then you verify them, either with an external checker, like running the code or checking the math, or with learned reward models, and you train on what works. That lets you keep scaling in a way that's no longer tied to how much text humans have written. You're effectively scaling inference-time compute and search, and then distilling that back into the model.

The hard part, and this is where I think a lot of the research is going, is domains where verification isn't clean. In Go or in math, you know who won or whether the proof checks out. In open-ended tasks like writing, or research, or giving advice, the reward signal is much fuzzier, and if you're not careful you end up optimizing against a flawed proxy. So the question becomes how to build good evaluators and good environments for those domains.

So my overall take is that the data wall will slow the naive version of scaling, but it won't stop progress. It's pushing the field toward approaches where models learn from their own experience, and I'm actually quite optimistic about that, because historically that's where some of the biggest leaps have come from.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the data wall is real in the narrow sense: if you just keep scaling pretraining on human-written text, you eventually run out of high-quality tokens. The internet is finite, and most of the easy, clean data has already been consumed. So the pure "more web data, bigger model" recipe does hit diminishing returns.

But I don't think of it as a wall for progress. I think of it as a wall for one particular paradigm. The lesson from AlphaGo and AlphaZero was exactly this. With AlphaGo we started from human games, and that got us to a certain level. With AlphaZero we threw the human data away entirely and had the system generate its own experience through self-play, and it surpassed everything that came before it. The constraint was never the amount of human data. The constraint was whether you had a learning loop that could produce its own signal.

So the interesting question for language models is: where does the signal come from once you've exhausted imitation? And I think the answer is reinforcement learning and search. Any domain where you can verify an outcome, whether that's mathematics, code, formal proofs, games, simulated environments, you can generate essentially unlimited training experience. The model proposes, something checks, and the model learns from the result. That's a fundamentally different scaling axis from scraping more text. You're trading data for compute, and compute is something we know how to scale.

The harder part is the domains where verification is fuzzy. Writing, judgment, taste, long-horizon planning in the real world. There, synthetic data can help, but you have to be careful because a model training on its own unfiltered outputs tends to drift and collapse. You need some grounding, whether that's a verifier, a human in the loop, or real interaction with an environment.

So my honest view is that the data wall will slow the specific trend of pretraining scaling, and it's already forcing the field to shift. But I think that shift, toward models that learn from their own experience rather than from a static snapshot of what humans wrote, is actually the more important direction anyway. It's what got us to superhuman performance in games, and I expect it's what gets us there in reasoning too.

astra-6.text:
I think the data wall is a real constraint if we assume that progress has to come from training on more and more human-generated text. But I don’t think that’s the only way forward. A model can also learn by trying things, getting feedback, and improving from that experience.

Games are a useful example: you don’t need an unlimited supply of human games if a system can play against itself and learn from the outcome. The interesting question is how to bring that kind of learning to more general tasks. With coding, for example, you can run a program and check whether it works.

The challenge is that generating more data isn’t enough on its own. You need some reliable way to tell whether what you generated is good. So I think the data wall shifts the emphasis toward reinforcement learning and environments that provide useful feedback. It may constrain the current recipe, but it doesn’t necessarily put a ceiling on progress.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the data wall is a real constraint if we assume that progress has to come from training on more human-written text. But I don’t think that’s the only way these systems can improve. They can also generate experience, interact with environments, and learn from feedback.

Games provide a useful example: you have a set of rules, and through self-play you can discover strategies that nobody explicitly put into the training data. The challenge with language models is that it’s much harder to determine whether an answer is actually good. In mathematics or coding, you can often verify a result, so there’s a clearer signal for learning. For more open-ended tasks, that signal is less straightforward.

So I think the data wall will change how we scale. Generating more text by itself isn’t enough; you need a process that can distinguish useful new experience from mistakes and learn from that.
